Larvae of Spodoptera frugiperda progress through six distinct instars before pupation, with female head capsule widths providing a reliable metric for staging development. First-instar females exhibit a head capsule width of 0.035 cm , a measurement that increases with each subsequent moult. By the second instar, the head capsule reaches 0.057 cm , and by the third instar it expands to 0.087 cm . This pattern of incremental growth continues through the later larval stages, reflecting the sclerotised nature of the lepidopteran cranium. Pupation marks a critical developmental transition, and the body length of larvae at this stage reaches 16.25/10 cm , a value derived from individuals reared under controlled laboratory conditions. The wet weight of pupae obtained from caterpillars fed an artificial diet averages 0.2889 grams , a measure that provides a useful baseline for comparing nutritional quality across different rearing substrates.

When maintained at a constant temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the duration of individual instars in Spodoptera frugiperda follows a predictable pattern that reflects the species' rapid development under optimal thermal conditions. The first larval instar lasts 2.57 days  at 25 °C [T = 25 °C], while the second instar is slightly shorter at 2.07 days  at 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. Instar three requires 2.13 days  at 25 °C [T = 25 °C] to complete, a duration that closely matches the second instar. The fourth instar extends to 2.48 days  at 25 °C [T = 25 °C], a stage of particular interest because it coincides with the attainment of puberty in females, as indicated by head capsule measurements. The fifth and sixth instars each occupy 2.57 days  at 25 °C [T = 25 °C] and 2.13 days  at 25 °C [T = 25 °C], respectively, before the larva enters the prepupal phase. Cumulatively, the total larval development under these conditions is relatively compressed, a life-history trait typical of many noctuids that exploit ephemeral host resources.

Sexual maturation in female Spodoptera frugiperda is linked to a specific developmental milestone during the fourth larval instar. At this stage, the head capsule width reaches 0.129 cm , and this same measurement defines the head capsule at puberty (0.129 cm) [Lp = 0.129 cm], confirming that instar four represents the point of gonadal activation. Under a thermal regime of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the time at puberty since birth is 9.25 days [tp = 9.25 days], a relatively early onset of reproductive competence compared to many other lepidopteran species. This rapid maturation is ecologically advantageous for a migratory pest species, allowing females to begin mating and ovipositing soon after adult eclosion. The fifth-instar head capsule expands to 0.189 cm , and by the final larval stage, sixth-instar females display a head capsule width of 0.28 cm , the largest recorded among the feeding stages prior to pupation. These morphometric data collectively illustrate the strategy of directing resources toward rapid somatic growth and early reproductive maturity.

Embryonic development and emergence in Spodoptera frugiperda are strongly influenced by environmental temperature, with cooler conditions prolonging developmental milestones. At 22 °C [T = 22 °C], the age at birth, defined as the time from oviposition to larval hatching, is 4.4 days [ab = 4.4 days]. This extended incubation period at lower temperatures likely reflects reduced metabolic rates within the embryonated egg, a pattern observed across many lepidopteran species. The time since birth at pupation under these cooler conditions is 27.5 days , substantially longer than what would be expected at warmer temperatures, illustrating the pronounced thermal sensitivity of larval growth. at a temperature of 22 °C [T = 22 °C]Furthermore, the total duration of the pupal stage, including both the prepupal and the quiescent metamorphic phase, amounts to 11.57 days  at 25 °C [T = 25 °C], though the time since pupation at emergence extends to 14.6 days since pupation  at 22 °C [T = 22 °C], highlighting the decelerating effect of sub-optimal thermal conditions on holometabolic reorganisation.

Comparing developmental rates across thermal environments provides insight into the adaptive plasticity of Spodoptera frugiperda, a species that colonises both tropical and temperate regions. Under the 25 °C [T = 25 °C] regime, the fourth-instar maturation at 9.25 days since birth [tp = 9.25 days since birth] contrasts sharply with the 27.5 day  total larval duration at 22 °C [T = 22 °C] from birth to pupation, revealing that cooler temperatures disproportionately affect overall development despite a constant proportional allocation of time to early maturation stages. This thermal sensitivity has direct implications for population dynamics in seasonal environments, where cooler springs may delay the emergence of the first generation. The consistent relationship between head capsule width and instar number provides a reliable tool for field ecologists assessing developmental stage distributions in natural populations. Such morphometric data remain essential for constructing accurate phenological models of this economically significant pest.
